analysis.one_liner: Lets small businesses and the self-employed pool together to buy private health plans, with a tax credit to help pay.
analysis.headline: The SHOP Act, a bipartisan bill to let small businesses and the self-employed buy private health plans together at lower rates, was referred to four House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The SHOP Act would have created a nationwide purchasing pool, run by the Department of Health and Human Services, where small businesses with up to 100 employees and self-employed people could buy private health plans together, instead of each small buyer negotiating alone. Insurers in the pool could not refuse coverage to eligible enrollees or charge more based on health status, gender, or claims history, and employers with 50 or fewer full-time workers would get a tax credit of up to about $1,000 per employee toward premiums. It was introduced with bipartisan support but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and employees of small businesses with 1 to 100 workers, and self-employed people earning at least $5,000 net or $15,000 gross from self-employment [S3]. Today a solo plumber or a 12-person shop buys insurance alone, on rates that can be set by health status; under this bill they would buy through a national pool where insurers cannot reject them or price them by health, gender, or claims history, and employers with 50 or fewer full-time workers would get a tax credit toward the premium [S3]. Insurers would gain millions of potential new customers through guaranteed contracts, cushioned by risk corridors that reimburse them if plan costs run above target in the first three years [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a nationwide purchasing pool administered by HHS where employers with 1 to 100 employees, and self-employed individuals, can buy private health plans, so small buyers get the pricing leverage that large employers already have.
Bars insurers in the pool from varying premiums based on health status, gender, claims experience, or class of business, and cuts the preexisting-condition exclusion period to 6 months.
Guarantees that any eligible employee or self-employed person who picks a plan cannot be refused coverage by the issuer.

Provides a tax credit of roughly $1,000 per employee with self-only coverage and $2,000 per employee with family coverage, largest for firms with 10 or fewer employees, payable in advance during the year.
Lets employees keep their plan for at least as long as COBRA continuation coverage if they lose their job, paying 102 percent of the premium.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the small-employer tax credit, the public education campaign, and the program's administration, all left as open-ended appropriations [S3]. Insurers in the pool would give up the ability to set premiums based on health status, gender, or claims experience, and to impose long preexisting-condition exclusions [S3]. States would lose their benefit mandates for nationwide plans sold in the pool [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; insurers lose health-based pricing

drawbacks.text: The tax credit phases down sharply with size: employers with 10 or fewer full-time employees get the full amount, those with more than 50 get nothing, which could discourage a small firm from hiring past a threshold.
For nationwide plans, state-mandated benefit laws would not apply, so a single federal benefit package would override state coverage requirements that states and consumer groups had fought for.
The Administrator would be barred from negotiating premiums with insurers and from excluding any issuer that meets the contract terms, limiting the pool's bargaining power over prices.

The bill itself directed the oversight board to monitor adverse selection between the new pool and the state-regulated market, acknowledging that a pool drawing in sicker, higher-cost enrollees could push premiums up for everyone in it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill was a fairly balanced deal: small businesses and the self-employed would have gained a pool with bargaining leverage, guaranteed enrollment, and a tax credit, while private insurers would have gained millions of potential new customers through contracts they could not be excluded from, softened by risk corridors that limited their downside in the first three years [S3]. The real costs were federal spending on the credit and administration, the loss of health-based pricing by insurers, and the preemption of state benefit mandates for nationwide plans [S3]. The credit's steep phase-out could also have discouraged small employers from crossing employee-count thresholds [S3]. The main cost to the public was not any flaw in the design but that the bill never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to even be debated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees on the day it was introduced and its subcommittee referrals in the following month, then nothing more ever happened; it died in committee when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Kind introduced the Small Business Health Options Program Act on May 12, 2009, with an original slate of cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, the House referred it to four committees: Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Rules.
In the following month it was referred to two subcommittees, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after that.
The bill attracted 61 cosponsors, 40 Democrats and 21 Republicans, but never reached a vote in either chamber.
The bill's congressional page records no further action for the remainder of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The small-group insurance status quo: insurers kept pricing small-business coverage as before, and no one paid for the bill's tax credit or gained its pool. Small businesses and the self-employed are the ones who never got the help the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Ron Kind
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with an original bipartisan group of 20 cosponsors.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Ways and Means, Rules)
against.role: Chairs of the four committees the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the congressional record shows no committee action after the June 2009 subcommittee referrals, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 40 of 253 House Democrats and 21 of 178 House Republicans cosponsored, and no vote ever occurred to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill makes private insurers the permanent channel for small-business coverage: the Administrator must contract with issuers, cannot exclude any qualified issuer, and cannot negotiate premiums, and risk corridors would reimburse insurers whose costs run above target in 2012-2014 [S3]. In exchange, insurers lose the ability to price by health status, gender, or claims history inside the pool [S3].
The bill lets issuers keep using licensed agents and brokers, and creates competitively bid contracts for private entities to collect premiums and administer enrollment regionally [S3].

Firms with 50 or fewer full-time employees would qualify for a health insurance tax credit, and all firms with up to 100 employees could join the pool [S3]. This is a constituent group as much as an industry, and the bill is written around their cost problem.
